newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy Sept CPI seen falling to 3.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy Sept CPI seen falling to 3.3 pct.

text.p: Italy's inflation rate should continue to fall in September even some grey clouds could start to emerge over the next few months, a Reuter poll of analysts showed on Wednesday.

Analysts polled by Reuters saw inflation rising on average 0.1/0.2 percent monthly and 3.2/3.3 percent yearly from a 0.1 and 3.4 percent rise in August. In September 1995, CPI rose 0.3 percent and 5.8 percent.
Preliminary CPI data from the 10 Italian sample cities will be issued on September 23 and 24. National statistics body Istat will publish the final national data on October 4.

Favouring this month's CPI is weak consumer demand and the fact that commodity prices have not yet been affected by petrol price hikes this summer. But the sectors of clothing, education (due to a back to school effect) and restaurants and bars could all have a negative effect, analysts said.

The only uncertainty lies over telephone tariffs. "If, as it appears, the utility decree is postponed to end-September, the reduction in telephone charges will not take place this month. Istat cannot count on a reduction which has not yet been approved," Giuseppe Abbotto, analyst at Indosuez, in Milan said.
The government earlier this year said it would approve a decree reducing telephone tariffs by the start of September.

"(The CPI data) should be a neutral but should continue to show that there are no medium-term inflation pressures. The real test will be further out in the year," said Marco Ratti, economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana (BCI).
"Consumer demand is very cautious and this makes it difficult for wholesale producers to make unjustified price increases", Pio De Gregorio of NatWest in Milan said.

"The recent hike in oil prices has apparently not yet filtered through to petrol and energy prices", Bank of America said in a research note. "Also some tariff increases like rail travel costs have been postponed to October and as a result September data should mainly reflect the underlying inflation trend, which remains benign".
"Food prices should continue to behave well, unwinding much of the rises we saw in 1995 and the first half of 1996," Bank of America added.
